approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would ban betting on the result of a lottery or keno draw.
It would prohibit gambling providers from offering such betting services to people in Australia.
The ban would start six months after the bill becomes law.
The bill would add a prohibition on betting on the outcome of Australian and overseas lottery draws.
The bill would clarify that keno-type lotteries are included in the prohibition.
The bill would delay the start of the prohibition for six months after royal assent.
State and territory governments, newsagencies, official lottery agents, and other small businesses in Australia.

Labor supported the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Lottery Betting) Bill 2018 to ban synthetic lotteries like Lottoland, citing risks to state revenues, small businesses (e.g., newsagents), and consumers, and arguing the Commonwealth is best placed to implement a national ban. The speaker noted state-level prohibitions in the Northern Territory, South Australia, and Tasmania, and referenced an ACCC investigation request into potentially misleading representations by lottery betting providers.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment (Lottery Betting) Bill 2018 is supported as it bans synthetic lottery betting, targeting operators like Lottoland that avoid Australian taxes by basing themselves in Gibraltar, thereby protecting state revenues and small businesses from lost income.

The speaker argued in support of the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Lottery Betting) Bill 2018, which would prohibit lottery and keno betting services to Australians, citing that traditional lotteries contribute over $1.1 billion annually in state taxes and support thousands of small businesses like newsagencies, whereas offshore services like Lottoland (based in Gibraltar) pay no Australian taxes and harm local retailers.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment (Lottery Betting) Bill 2018 was supported to give greater protections against synthetic lotteries like Lottoland, citing Australia's $1,300 per capita gambling losses and a 7.7% increase in total expenditure to $22.7 billion in 2014-15. Labor had requested an ACCC investigation into lottery betting companies and consulted with stakeholders including the newsagents peak body.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment (Lottery Betting) Bill 2018 should prohibit lottery betting services, which allow customers to bet on outcomes without buying an official lottery ticket, to reduce problem gambling and protect newsagencies; the speaker noted that 200,000 Australians have a high-level gambling problem, 650,000 account holders gamble via mobile, and 4,000 newsagencies earn $350 million in commissions from official lottery sales.

The speaker supported the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Lottery Betting) Bill 2018, arguing it would create a level playing field by requiring companies like Lottoland to meet the same tax and regulatory obligations as existing providers, while also addressing gambling addiction and consumer protection.

The speaker supported the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Lottery Betting) Bill 2018, citing that Australians lost nearly $24 billion to gambling in 2017 and that increased gambling opportunities lead to higher crime, domestic violence, and community harm. He also opposed a proposed casino in the Sunshine Coast electorate, noting unanimous community opposition and revealing 4,600 relevant documents from council and state government discussions.

The government argued the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Lottery Betting) Bill 2018 should pass because online synthetic lottery and keno betting services undermine traditional lotteries, which generate over $350 million for some 4,000 newsagencies and support community services, and the Commonwealth must act to protect consumers and small businesses. The bill targets these betting services while leaving state and territory licensing arrangements untouched.
